issues.legal_issue: A defence asserting that property was held benami is not barred in a suit when both the suit and the defence were filed before the statutory prohibition came into force.
material_facts: The property transaction predated the statutory prohibition.
The suit was filed before the prohibition came into force.
The defendant raised the benami defence in a written statement filed before the prohibition came into force, although the trial judgment was delivered afterward.
issues.conclusion: The defendant was entitled to raise and prove the benami defence; the later delivery of the trial judgment did not make the statutory bar applicable to that defence.
issues.legal_principle: Section 4(2) of the Benami Transaction (Prohibition) Act, 1988 does not operate retrospectively to bar a benami defence already raised before the Act came into force. R. Rajagopal Reddy (Dead) by LRs. v. Padmini Chandrasekharan (Dead) by LRs. held that the Act is prospective, with limited operation in pending suits where the defence had not already been raised; it overruled Mithilesh Kumari v. Prem Behari Khare and was approved in Prabodh Chandra Ghosh v. Urmila Dassi and C. Gangacharan v. C. Narayanan.

predicates.benami_property_dispute: The proceeding is a property dispute in which a party claims that the person named on the title held the property benami.
predicates.suit_filed_before_prohibition: The suit was filed before the statutory prohibition on benami claims came into force.
predicates.benami_defence_raised_before_prohibition: The defendant raised the benami defence before the statutory prohibition came into force.

issues.definition: When a property dispute includes a benami defence raised before the prohibition came into force, that defence is not barred merely because the case continued afterward.

issues.legal_issue: The presumption that property bought in an unmarried daughter's name was purchased for her benefit can be rebutted by evidence that the purchaser acquired and controlled it for his own benefit.
material_facts: The father purchased the property in his minor, unmarried daughter's name and paid the purchase price.
The father retained the original title deeds, mortgaged the property to raise money for improvements, paid taxes and other charges, and let out portions of the property and collected rent.

The courts below found that the purchase was motivated by the father's belief that buying property in his daughter's name would bring him prosperity, and that the surrounding circumstances and his later conduct supported a benami transaction.
The father later bequeathed the property to his daughter and two sons; the Court considered that act consistent with his treating the property as his own.
The trial and appellate courts concurrently found that the daughter was a benamidar and that the father was the real owner.
issues.conclusion: The presumption in favour of the unmarried daughter was rebutted by cogent evidence, and the concurrent finding that the father was the real owner was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3(2) of the Benami Transaction (Prohibition) Act, 1988 presumes, unless the contrary is proved, that property purchased in the name of a person's wife or unmarried daughter was purchased for her benefit. The presumption is rebuttable by evidence or other material. The Court treated the payment of the purchase price, retention of title documents, mortgage and improvement of the property, payment of taxes, collection of rents, motive, surrounding circumstances, and subsequent conduct as relevant evidence.

rule.if: property_title_dispute and property_bought_in_unmarried_daughters_name and purchaser_paid_purchase_price and purchaser_retained_title_deeds and purchaser_mortgaged_property_for_improvements and purchaser_paid_property_charges and purchaser_collected_rent and purchaser_personal_motive_evidence

predicates.property_title_dispute: The proceeding concerns competing claims to ownership of property.
predicates.property_bought_in_unmarried_daughters_n: A parent purchased the property in the name of an unmarried daughter.
predicates.purchaser_paid_purchase_price: The parent paid the purchase price from the parent's own funds.
predicates.purchaser_retained_title_deeds: The parent kept the original title documents.
predicates.purchaser_mortgaged_property_for_improve: The parent mortgaged the property to obtain funds for its improvement.
predicates.purchaser_paid_property_charges: The parent paid taxes or other charges relating to the property.
predicates.purchaser_collected_rent: The parent let out the property or parts of it and collected the rent.
predicates.purchaser_personal_motive_evidence: Evidence showed that the parent bought the property in the daughter's name for a personal motive rather than to benefit her.

issues.definition: When a parent buys property in an unmarried daughter's name but pays for and controls it and the evidence supports a personal-benefit motive, the presumption that the purchase benefited the daughter is rebutted.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court cannot set aside concurrent findings of fact in a second appeal without a legally sufficient basis for interference, such as perversity or failure to consider important evidence.
material_facts: The trial court and first appellate court made concurrent findings, based on pleadings and oral and documentary evidence, that the transaction was benami.

The High Court reversed those findings in second appeal based on its own contrary view, including a representation made by counsel and the father's will, without adequately considering the evidence or the lower courts' findings.
The Supreme Court found the lower courts' findings reasoned and supported by the evidence, and found no perversity, overlooked important evidence, or other sufficient ground for setting them aside.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in interfering with the concurrent findings in second appeal; its judgment was set aside and the lower courts' judgments were affirmed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a High Court may interfere with concurrent findings in a second appeal only on a sufficient legal basis; concurrent findings supported by evidence and sound reasoning cannot be displaced merely by substituting a contrary factual view. Interference may be justified where, for example, an important admission or other important evidence was overlooked. The Court relied on Deva (Dead) Through LRs. v. Sajjan Kumar (Dead) by LRs., Sayeda Akhtar v. Abdul Ahad, Saraswathi v. S. Ganapathy, and Gangajal Kunwar v. Sarju Pandey (Dead) by LRs.

rule.if: second_appeal and concurrent_supported_fact_findings and high_court_reversed_findings_without_considering_record and no_sufficient_ground_for_interference

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding before the High Court is a second appeal from a decision based on factual findings.
predicates.concurrent_supported_fact_findings: The trial court and first appellate court reached the same factual findings after considering the evidence, and those findings have evidentiary support and sound reasoning.
predicates.high_court_reversed_findings_without_con: The High Court displaced the concurrent findings without adequately considering the evidence and the lower courts' reasoning.
predicates.no_sufficient_ground_for_interference: The record discloses no perversity, overlooked important evidence, or other legally sufficient basis for disturbing the concurrent findings.

issues.definition: When a High Court in a second appeal reverses supported concurrent factual findings without considering the record and without a sufficient ground for interference, that reversal is improper.
